newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi says innocent, President defends him.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi says innocent, President defends him.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, facing possible trial for alleged business malpractice, said on Sunday the truth had been badly distorted.
Prodi faces a preliminary court hearing in January to decide whether he should be tried for alleged irregularities while chairman of state holding company IRI three years ago.
"There has been a false and deceitful reading of the facts," Prodi told reporters in his northern home town of Bologna.
"It's an incredible reading of the judicial documents."

The latest legal bombshell in Italy, where magistrates have been investigating alleged corruptione and graft in politics and big business for four years, broke last week when news agencies leaked that a Rome magistrate wanted to try Prodi for alleged conflict of interest and abuse of office during his time at IRI.
Prodi, who became prime minister in May, has said he is confident the case will not go to trial and he is innocent of wrongdoing.
He has been given high-level backing by President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro.
Scalfaro, answering reporters' questions during a trip to Egypt on Saturday, declared: "The Prime Minister has given extremely clear replies. For now, there is no problem."
But far-right leader Gianfranco Fini blasted Scalfaro on Sunday, saying he was guilty of unwelcome meddling, particularly since he is also head of the magistrates' ruling body.
"The President of the Republic should not judge whether Prodi's statements have been sufficient and exhaustive or not. he told state television from the northern city of Turin.
Corriere della Sera, one of Italy's top-selling newspapers, also said Scalfaro was unwise not to have remained impartial.
In a rare unsigned, front-page editorial headlined "One word too many", it said it could not remember a head of state taking such a decisive stance in favour of a member of the government.

The case surrounding Prodi centres on the sale by IRI of food group Cirio in 1993, in which Rome deputy public prosecutor Giuseppa Geremia alleges that IRI granted the buyer, Fis.Vi, an unjust advantage.
Prodi also faces a charge of conflict of interest over a consultancy he held with Anglo-Dutch company Unilever, which bought the group's oil business soon afterwards.
But he dismissed the allegations. "I'm being accused of something that happened a month before I became chairman of IRI," Prodi said.
"I have nothing else to say. When the foundations are wrong, all the rest is wrong."
Prodi's legal headaches come at a tricky time politically as his centre-left government is seeking parliamentary approval for an unpopular "Euro-tax" to prepare for European monetary union.

Scalfaro had already said that, in the event of Prodi falling, he would do his utmost to avoid yet another general election. But Massimo D'Alema, head of the biggest party in the government, said last week new polls vote would be the only solution in that case.
Italy's opposition leader, ex-prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, is already on trial in two separate corruption cases. He also denies wrongdoing.
